scope: Reviewed authored English directions only. No student data.

records.text: Control the assembled hand. In this guide. This program uses four working servos: motor1, motor2, motor4 and motor5. Two knobs and four buttons control them. Motor3 is broken and disabled. A servo moves toward a chosen position. Find knobs 1 and 2 and buttons S1 to S4. Leave knob 3 unused. Keep the model disconnected while writing code. Check. You can point to the six active controls. Motor3 and its A three knob are not used. Keep the existing wiring.

Open your team sketch. Ardweeno I D E > File. A sketch is an Ardweeno program. Work in one saved team copy so teammates do not replace each other’s changes. Open the latest numbered team sketch. Save a new numbered copy before editing. For a first session, create and save RoboticHand_01 in Ardweeno I D E. Check. You have one editable sketch with a numbered name.

Keep two empty sections. In the sketch editor. setup() runs once when the board starts. loop() repeats while the board runs. Curly braces mark the start and end of each section. For a new sketch, keep the two empty sections shown below. When continuing, find these sections in your existing code instead of adding duplicates. Check. One setup() and one loop(), each with { and }. If later code is already present, compare it and add only missing lines; do not duplicate it.

Name the four working servos. At the very top, before setup(). #include <Servo.h> loads the servo instructions. Servo names the motor type; motor1 is the name we give one motor. The semicolon ; ends each Servo line. Add the include line and the four working motor names above setup. Check. The sketch names motor1, motor2, motor4 and motor5. There is no motor3 object.

Name the buttons and starting values. Below the four working Servo lines, before setup(). const int names a fixed pin number. int stores a number that can change. The = sign stores the number on its right in the name on its left. Add these six lines below the Servo names and above setup(). Check. S1–S4 name pins 2–5. middleAngle starts at 125 and baseAngle at 86.

Prepare the four buttons. At the start of setup(), inside its braces. input pull up makes an unpressed button read high and a pressed button read low with the checked wiring. Add these four lines immediately after void setup() {. Move any old attach lines to the later signal-pin step. Check. All four buttons use input pull up. No motor is attached yet.

Load motor one before signals start. Inside setup(), after the four pinMode lines. analogRead reads knob one. map changes its 0-1023 reading into a 0-57 command. write stores that target. Before attach, this stores a target without enabling motor signals. Add these three lines before any attach line. Check. Motor1 has a starting target from A one, within 0-57, before its signals start.

Load the second knob target. Inside setup(), after the motor1 starting lines. Motor2 needs its own bounded starting target. Use read, map, write again. Motor3 is disabled, so do not add an A three group. Add this motor2 group before any attach line. Check. A two supplies motor2 with a 0-180 starting command. A three remains unused.

Load the middle and base targets. Inside setup(), after the two active knob targets. The buttons use remembered commands. Their starting values are middleAngle 125 and baseAngle 86. Add these two write lines before all four attach lines. Check. All four working motors have targets loaded before any servo signals are enabled.

Match motors to signal pins. At the end of setup(), after all four starting write lines. attach enables servo signals on a pin. Loading every target first prevents the library default from being the first commanded pulse. Place these four attach lines after the starting targets and before setup closes. Remove any earlier copies and every motor3 attach. Check. Only D6, D7, D9 and D10 are attached. D8 is never attached. Every starting write comes before the first attach.

Check the setup code. Ardweeno I D E > Verify, the checkmark button. Verify checks whether the computer can compile your sketch. Compile means translating code into instructions the board can run. Verify does not run the hand. Choose Ardweeno Uno for the confirmed FNK0059-compatible control board. Choose Verify with the model disconnected. Check. The I D E finishes without a compilation error.

Make knob one control motor one. At the start of loop(), inside its existing braces. setup reads the knobs once for startup. loop reads them again and again so the motors follow later knob changes. Add these three lines in order. Check. A one supplies pot1, angle1 holds the scaled value, and motor1 receives angle1.

Make knob two control motor two. Inside loop(), after the three knob-one lines. Use read, map, write again for motor2. Motor3 is broken, so A three is not read and D8 is not driven. Add this motor2 group after the knob-one lines inside loop. Remove the old A three and motor3 group if present. Check. A two controls motor2 with 0-180 commands. The sketch has no A three read or motor3 write.

Make S3 move down. Inside loop(), after the knobs. S3 moves the middle joint down by increasing its command. bool stores true or false. The first two lines read S3 and S1 once. and means and; not means not. The if runs only when S3 is pressed and S1 is not. Replace the old S3 block with these button readings and the guarded increase block. Check. S3 alone moves the middle joint down. Its command increases up to 160. Both pressed skips this block.

Make S1 move up. Inside loop(), after the complete S3 block. S1 moves the middle joint up by decreasing its command. This block uses the same saved button readings. It runs only when S1 is pressed and S3 is not. -- subtracts one. Replace the old S1 block with this guarded decrease block. Check. S1 alone moves the middle joint up. Its command decreases to 90. Both middle buttons pressed leaves the target unchanged.

Make S4 move down. Inside loop(), after the complete S1 block. S4 moves the base joint down by increasing its command. This block runs only when S4 is pressed and S2 is not. Replace the old S4 block with these two readings and the guarded increase block, after the S1 block. Check. S4 alone moves the base joint down. Its command increases up to 176. Both base buttons pressed skips this block.

Make S2 move up. Inside loop(), after the complete S4 block. S2 moves the base joint up by decreasing its command. This block runs only when S2 is pressed and S4 is not. The lower limit keeps baseAngle at or above zero. Replace the old S2 block with this guarded decrease block, after the S4 block. Check. S2 alone moves the base joint up. Its command decreases to 0. Both base buttons pressed leaves the target unchanged.

Finish and verify the full program. At the end of loop(), then Ardweeno I D E > Verify. A short pause ends each pass through loop(). Verify checks whether the complete code can be translated for the selected board. Add delay(15); after the complete S2 block, before loop() closes. Choose Verify and save the numbered sketch when it passes. Check. One setup, one loop, all four guarded button blocks and every limit check compile without errors.

Check the model before testing. At the assembled model. Servo signals can move the mechanism as soon as an uploaded program starts. Code numbers alone cannot establish safe physical movement. Before the first test, have the teacher check the Freenove control board, module switches, servo power, motor3 isolation, starting pose, active knob positions and allowed movement. Check. The model has its initial hardware check. Your complete program passes Verify. Repeat the hardware check if the wiring, power or movement limits change.

Send the code to Ardweeno. Ardweeno I D E > Upload. Upload sends the saved program to Ardweeno. Editing code on the computer does not change the program running on the board. The hand can move as soon as the new program starts. Connect the checked model by U S B. Select Ardweeno Uno and its U S B port. Choose Upload to send your complete saved program to Ardweeno. Test it after the I D E reports that sending finished. Check. Ardweeno runs the version you just sent. Repeat Upload and the affected test after every modification to the complete program.

Observe startup after sending. At the checked model. Correct startup code still sends targets that may differ from the current physical pose. Only a real test shows the movement. After sending the complete program to Ardweeno, watch its starting movement from the checked pose and knob settings. Record what happens in Test and improvement. Check. Your note identifies the sketch version, starting settings, actual movement and any strain or unexpected motion.

Test and record the two knobs. At the checked model, with the teacher. Testing one input at a time shows which input caused the response. A correct compile cannot tell us which physical part moved. Turn knob 1 slowly within the checked range and watch motor1. Repeat separately with knob 2 and motor2. Record both actual responses under Test and improvement. Check. Each note names the sketch version, expected motor, actual movement and any problem. Knob 3 remains unused.

Test and record the four buttons. At the checked model, with the teacher. A single pressed button changes one remembered command. Releasing it stops further changes from that button. The servo remains active and may still reach or hold its last target. Try S1, S2, S3 and S4 separately within the checked range. Release each before trying the next. Add each actual response to the same test note. Check. S1/S3 command motor4 in opposite directions; S2/S4 command motor5 in opposite directions. Your notes say what actually moved.

Check opposite buttons together. At the checked model, with the teacher. When both buttons of one pair are pressed, both guarded blocks are skipped. This keeps that joint command unchanged. It is not a power-off or an emergency stop. After the single-button tests, briefly hold S1 and S3 together at a settled checked position. Release both. Repeat with S2 and S4. Record each result. Check. Each pair leaves its joint target unchanged. After releasing both, a single button still works.

Change, send and test again. Ardweeno I D E and your test note. Change one thing at a time so you can tell whether it helped. Ardweeno keeps running the old program until you send the new version. After each modification to the complete program, choose Verify. Save a new numbered version. Choose Upload to send it to Ardweeno. Repeat the same affected control test and record the result. Check. Each modification has a saved version, a successful Upload and a matching test result. Keep the previous result for comparison.

Explain the code in your team report. In your existing team report, under Project. Following one input through the code shows how the program produces an output. Under Project, explain one knob or button: input, value change, limit and motor. Keep the report headings Project; Research; Test and improvement; References. Check. Your explanation matches your saved code and test notes. A command limit is not a measured physical angle.

Save and share the tested version. Your computer file manager and existing team Drive folder. The next editor needs the real code and a clear note about what was checked. Save the sketch. Compress its whole numbered folder as a ZIP and upload it to the team folder. Check that it contains the matching .ino. Tell the next editor the filename and whether hardware tests ran. Check. The team has the latest editable program, its ZIP and the matching report. Earlier versions remain available.

Check your complete program. Final reference · Ardweeno I D E. Use this full sketch to check the program you built one section at a time. Compare your saved sketch with the complete code below. Keep motors 1, 2, 4 and 5. Motor3 stays disabled. Check. All four starting targets come before attach. Opposing buttons leave that joint target unchanged. There is no A three read or D8 attachment.
